report:
**Conclusion: your “no” is substantially correct.** Whole-body vibration (WBV) has *not* been shown convincingly to prevent osteoporotic fractures. The fracture-specific evidence is especially thin: a 2017 systematic review/meta-analysis found fewer falls, but only **one** included study reported fractures and its reduction was **not statistically significant**. Thus, fracture prevention remains unproven.  
https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/7/12/e018342

Why there is some uncertainty: WBV might improve balance/leg function and therefore reduce falls, a pathway that could reduce fractures. Some trials and meta-analyses also report modest bone-mineral-density (BMD) benefits in selected postmenopausal women, depending on vibration settings and protocol. For example, a 2020 randomized trial reported improved lumbar/femoral BMD, but BMD is a *surrogate*, not evidence that fractures are prevented.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32868028/  
https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0166774

Conversely, trial results on BMD are inconsistent. A 12-month randomized trial in postmenopausal women found no improvement in BMD or bone structure with WBV (alongside calcium and vitamin D).  
https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/0003-4819-155-10-201111150-00005

**Bottom line:** WBV may be a reasonable *adjunct exercise option* for some people—particularly if it improves strength, balance, or adherence to activity—but it should not be presented as an effective fracture-prevention treatment for osteoporosis. It should not replace proven fracture-reduction measures: clinician-directed osteoporosis medication when indicated, adequate calcium/vitamin D, resistance/weight-bearing and balance exercise, and fall-risk reduction.
